subtype: Approach: experiment and measure over two weeks [Action]
passage: Monday. Arohi could not decide how to study Maths, so she chose to test it. Week one: read solved examples first, then try the problems. On Friday Pankaj wrote out a ten-question quiz in his neat hand, and she noted her score in a table: six out of ten. Monday of week two. New method: attempt the problems first and check the solutions afterwards. On the second Friday Pankaj's quiz came again: nine out of ten. Arohi laid the two rows side by side. Attempting first was clearly better for her, even though it felt slower and messier. She circled the nine and told Pankaj, "Same time next week."

qa.q: What score did Arohi get in the first quiz?
qa.a: Arohi scored six out of ten.

qa.q: What did Arohi feel about the second method?
qa.a: Uncertain at first because it felt slower and messier, but convinced by the scores.

qa.q: What could Arohi do if a topic fits neither method?
qa.a: Test a third method for two weeks and compare, because the same measure gives a fair comparison.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Arohi's experiment?
qa.a: As a useful project, since he set the quizzes and saw the difference in the results.

grounding: A student tries two study methods, tracks quiz scores for two weeks, and keeps the method that clearly gave better results.

subtype: Approach: experiment and measure over two weeks [Action]
passage: Nandini, your Ujjwal Mama was a poor Maths student long before he became an engineer, did you know that? Class 11, calculus, and I was failing. My friends argued: some said read all the solved examples first, some said try the problems yourself and only then look. I didn't know who was right, so I tested it. For two weeks of differentiation, I read the solved examples before every exercise. For the next two weeks, on integration, I tried problems first and checked after. Every Saturday our teacher gave a ten-mark quiz, and I wrote my score in the back of my notebook. Reading first: 4, then 5. Trying first: 7, then 8. Not even close. So I kept trying first, all the way to the board exam.

qa.q: What were Ujjwal's quiz scores when trying problems first?
How might young Ujjwal have felt while his friends argued about methods?
qa.a: He probably felt confused and unsure whom to believe, which is why he decided to test both himself.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the method decision reliable?
qa.a: Writing down every Saturday quiz score for each method, so the choice rested on clear numbers rather than friends' opinions.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ujjwal had just followed one friend's advice?
qa.a: He might have kept reading examples first and stayed around 4 or 5 out of ten, never knowing a better method existed.

grounding: An elder recalls testing two study methods for two weeks each, tracking quiz scores and keeping the clearly better one.

subtype: Approach: experiment and measure over two weeks [Action]
passage: Shreya had one hour a night for Chemistry, after her mother left for the night shift and her little brother was finally asleep. With a failing grade and so little time, she couldn't afford a method that didn't work. Her friend Nazia swore by reading the solved examples first. Their teacher said try first, then check. So Shreya split the fortnight: week one, examples first; week two, problems first. Every Friday the class had a twenty-mark quiz, and she wrote her scores on the inside cover of her notebook. Examples first: 8. Problems first: 14. She looked at the two numbers for a long time. Nazia's way felt comfortable; it just didn't stick. From then on, her one hour started with a blank page and a problem.

qa.q: What did Shreya score in the week she tried problems first?
Why did Shreya look at the two numbers for a long time?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and a bit torn, since Nazia's comfortable method clearly scored lower than the harder one.

qa.q: What else could Shreya check to be surer of the result?
qa.a: Try the winning method for another week or two on a different chapter, so one good quiz isn't mistaken for a pattern.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel hearing that the examples-first method lost?
qa.a: Nazia may be a little disappointed or defensive, but might also become curious to try problems first.

grounding: Shows a student with little time comparing two methods over two weeks by quiz scores and keeping the clearly better one.
